nodes.name: Sunny-side-up shift counterexample
nodes.statement: Irreducibility of the sofic shift is essential: the Lanford-Ruelle theorem holds for shifts of finite type with no irreducibility assumption, but it is false in general for reducible sofic shifts. The simplest counterexample is the sunny-side-up shift (the set of sequences in $\{ 0,1 \}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ with at most a single $1$) with its unique shift-invariant measure.
nodes.statement_short: The sunny-side-up shift is a reducible sofic shift where Lanford-Ruelle fails, so irreducibility is essential.

nodes.name: Alphabet and full shift
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set with the discrete topology, to be thought of as an alphabet, and $\mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ be the \textit{full shift} with the product topology, with respect to which $\mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ is compact and metrizable.

nodes.name: Shift action
nodes.statement: The group $\mathbb{Z}$ acts naturally on $\mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ by the shift action $\sigma$, given by $(\sigma^n x)_0 = x_n$.

nodes.name: Shift space
nodes.statement: A \textit{shift space} is any closed, $\sigma$-invariant subset $X \subseteq \mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{Z}}$.

nodes.name: Language and words of length n
nodes.statement: For each $n \geq 1$, we write $\mathcal{B}_{n}(X)$ to denote the set of words of length $n$ in the language $\mathcal{B}(X)$ of $X$---that is, the set of patterns $w \in \mathcal{A}^{n}$ such that $x_{[0,n-1]} = w$ for some $x \in X$.

nodes.name: Cylinder set
nodes.statement: For $w \in \mathcal{A}^{n}$ we denote by $[w]_{i}$ the set of $x \in X$ with $x_{[i,i+n-1]} = w$.

nodes.name: Curtis-Hedlund-Lyndon theorem
nodes.statement: By the Curtis-Hedlund-Lyndon theorem, any such map $\pi$ is a sliding block code, induced by a map $\Pi: \mathcal{B}_m(X) \to \mathcal{B}_1(Y)$ for some $m \geq 1$.
assumptions: any such map $\pi$
conclusions: is a sliding block code, induced by a map $\Pi: \mathcal{B}_m(X) \to \mathcal{B}_1(Y)$ for some $m \geq 1$
nodes.statement_short: Every continuous shift-equivariant map between shift spaces is a sliding block code.

nodes.name: Recoding to a one-block code
nodes.statement: Up to a conjugacy of $X$, we can in fact assume that $\Pi$ maps symbols to symbols, i.e., $m=1$ (\cite{lind1995introduction}, Proposition 1.5.12).
assumptions: Up to a conjugacy of $X$
conclusions: $\Pi$ maps symbols to symbols, i.e., $m=1$

nodes.name: Factor code
nodes.statement: When $\pi: X \to Y$ is surjective, it is known as a \textit{factor} code, and $Y$ is a \textit{factor} of $X$.

nodes.name: Shift of finite type
differentia: defined by excluding a finite number of finite words
nodes.statement_short: A shift space defined by forbidding finitely many finite words.
nodes.label: SFT-shift

nodes.name: Sofic shift
nodes.statement:
[sofic shift]
A \textit{sofic shift} is any shift space that is a continuous factor of a shift of finite type.
differentia: a continuous factor of a shift of finite type
nodes.label: sofic-shift

nodes.name: Every shift of finite type is sofic
nodes.statement: Every shift of finite type is sofic, since the identity code is continuous (more generally, conjugacies preserve the class of shifts of finite type), but not every sofic shift has finite type.

nodes.name: Even shift
nodes.statement: An example of a shift that is sofic but not of finite type is the even shift, which is the shift $X \subset \{ 0,1 \}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ consisting of sequences in which $10^n1$ may appear only if $n$ is even.

nodes.name: Measures are Borel probability measures
nodes.statement: We will, in particular, consider measures on shift spaces, which will always be Borel probability measures.

nodes.name: Ergodic measure convention
nodes.statement: In particular, we will often refer to ergodic measures, and these will always be ergodic with respect to $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Gibbs relation
nodes.statement: The \textit{Gibbs relation} on a shift space $X$, also called the tail, asymptotic, or homoclinic relation, is the equivalence relation $\mathfrak{T}_X \subset X \times X$ such that $(x,y) \in \mathfrak{T}_X$ if and only if $x_{[-N,N]^c} = y_{[-N,N]^c}$ for some $N \geq 1$.
differentia: $(x,y) \in \mathfrak{T}_X$ if and only if $x_{[-N,N]^c} = y_{[-N,N]^c}$ for some $N \geq 1$
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Holonomy
nodes.statement: For Borel sets $A, B \subseteq X$, a \textit{holonomy} of $\mathfrak{T}_X$ is a Borel isomorphism $\psi: A \to B$ such that $(x, \psi(x)) \in \mathfrak{T}_X$ for all $x \in A$.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Nonsingular measure and saturation
nodes.statement:
We say that a measure $\mu$ on $X$ is $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular if for every Borel $A \subset X$ with $\mu(A) = 0$, we have $\mu(\mathfrak{T}_X(A)) = 0$, where the saturation $\mathfrak{T}_X(A)$ is defined as 
\[
\mathfrak{T}_X(A) = \{ x' \in X \, : \, \exists \, x \in A \text{ such that } (x,x') \in \mathfrak{T}_X      \}
\]
nodes.statement_short: A measure is nonsingular if the saturation of every null set under the Gibbs relation is null.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Radon-Nikodym derivative of holonomies is well-defined
nodes.statement: Note that if $\mu$ is $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular and $\psi: A \to B$ is a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_X$, then whenever $E \subset A$ has $\mu(E) = 0$, we have $\mu(\psi(E)) \leq \mu(\mathfrak{T}_X(E)) = 0$. In particular, the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{d(\mu \circ \psi)}{d\mu}$ is well-defined.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Feldman-Moore theorem (countable generating group of holonomies)
nodes.statement: We note that $\mathfrak{T}_{X}$ is generated by a countable group $\Gamma$ of holonomies, in the sense that $(x,x') \in \mathfrak{T}_{X}$ if and only if there exists $\gamma \in \Gamma$ with $\gamma(x) = x'$. This is a special case of the main theorem of \cite{feldman-moore-1977-equivalence}.
conclusions: $\mathfrak{T}_{X}$ is generated by a countable group $\Gamma$ of holonomies
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Swap holonomies psi_{u,v,a,b}
nodes.statement_short: The holonomy that swaps words u and v on [a,b] whenever the result stays in X, else does nothing.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Cocycle
nodes.statement: A (real, additive) \textit{cocycle} on $\mathfrak{T}_X$ is a Borel measurable function $\phi: \mathfrak{T}_X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\phi(x,y) + \phi(y,z) = \phi(x,z)$ for all $x,y,z \in X$ with $(x,y), (y,z) \in \mathfrak{T}_X$ (so that $(x,z) \in \mathfrak{T}_X$ as well).
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Radon-Nikodym cocycle
nodes.statement: Given a $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular measure $\mu$ on $X$, we say that a Borel function $D_{\mu,\mathfrak{T}_X}: \mathfrak{T}_X \to \mathbb{R}^+$ is a (multiplicative) \textit{Radon-Nikodym cocycle} on $\mathfrak{T}_X$ with respect to $\mu$ if the pushforward of $\mu$ by any holonomy $\psi: A \to B$ of $\mathfrak{T}_X$ satisfies $\frac{d(\mu \circ \psi)}{d\mu}(x) = D_{\mu,\mathfrak{T}_X}(x, \psi(x))$ for $\mu$-a.e. $x \in A$.
nodes.statement_short: The cocycle giving the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the pushforward of mu under every holonomy.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of the Radon-Nikodym cocycle
nodes.statement: It is routine to show that any $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular measure $\mu$ on $X$ has a $\mu$-a.e. unique Radon-Nikodym cocycle.
assumptions: any $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular measure $\mu$ on $X$
conclusions: has a $\mu$-a.e. unique Radon-Nikodym cocycle
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Gibbs measure
nodes.statement:
[Gibbs measure]
    Let $\mu$ be a $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular Borel measure on a shift space $X$, and let $\phi: \mathfrak{T}_X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cocycle. We say that $\mu$ is a \textit{Gibbs measure} if for any holonomy $\psi: A \to B$ of $\mathfrak{T}_X$, and $\mu$-a.e. $x \in A$, we have $D_{\mu, \mathfrak{T}_X}(x,\psi(x)) = \exp(\phi(x,\psi(x)))$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonsingular measure whose Radon-Nikodym cocycle equals exp of a given cocycle along every holonomy.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures
nodes.label: Gibbs-measure-defn

nodes.name: Gibbs measures as conformal measures
nodes.statement: To put it another way, a measure is by definition Gibbs if and only if it is nonsingular, and a nonsingular measure is Gibbs precisely with respect to the logarithm of its own Radon-Nikodym cocycle. These measures are also known as conformal measures in the literature \cite{borsato2020conformal, meyerovitch2013gibbs}.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Equivalence with the DLR definition of Gibbs measures
nodes.statement: In \cite{borsato2020conformal} it is shown, building on results of Kimura \cite{kimura-2015-thesis}, Keller \cite{keller1998equilibrium}, and others, that the definition of a Gibbs measure that we have given is equivalent to another well-known one involving the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations, in terms of which the theorems of Dobrushin (Theorem \ref{dobrushin}) and Lanford-Ruelle (Theorem \ref{lf}) were originally stated.
conclusions: the definition of a Gibbs measure that we have given is equivalent to another well-known one involving the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Not Gibbs in the sense of Bowen
nodes.statement: These Gibbs measures do not coincide, in general, with Gibbs measures in the sense of Bowen; see the second remark after Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} for further discussion.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Gibbs relation, cocycles, and Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Irreducibility
nodes.statement:
[irreducibility]
A shift space $X$ is irreducible if for every ordered pair of blocks $u, v \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ there is $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ so that $uwv \in \mathcal{B}(X)$.
differentia: for every ordered pair of blocks $u, v \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ there is $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ so that $uwv \in \mathcal{B}(X)$
nodes.label: defn-irred-z

nodes.name: Period
nodes.statement:
[period]
The \textit{period} of an irreducible sofic shift is the greatest common divisor of the least periods of its periodic points.
nodes.label: defn-aper

nodes.name: Strong irreducibility
nodes.statement:
[strong irreducibility]
A shift space $X$ is \textit{strongly irreducible} if there exists some $r \geq 1$ such that for any $u,v \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ and any $s \geq r$, there exists $w \in \mathcal{B}_s(X)$ with $uwv \in \mathcal{B}(X)$.
nodes.label: strong-irred-defn

nodes.name: Strong irreducibility equals mixing for SFTs
nodes.statement: A shift of finite type is strongly irreducible if and only if it is topologically mixing, if and only if it is irreducible and has period $1$.

nodes.name: Nonsingular measures on strongly irreducible shifts have full support
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a strongly irreducible shift space. Then any $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant nonsingular measure on $X$ has full support.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a strongly irreducible shift space.
conclusions: any $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant nonsingular measure on $X$ has full support
nodes.label: strong-irred-support

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant nonsingular measure on $X$. Let $r \geq 1$ be a witness for the strong irreducibility of $X$. Fix $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a < b$, and fix $w \in \mathcal{B}_{b-a}(X)$. By strong irreducibility, for each $n \geq 1$ and each $p, s \in \mathcal{B}_{n}(X)$, there exists $w' \in \mathcal{B}_{(b-a)+2r} (X)$ such that $w'_{[a,b]} = w$ and $p w' s \in \mathcal{B}(X)$.
By compactness, it follows that for every $x \in X$, there exists some $u \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ with $u_{[a,b]} = w$ and $x_{(-\infty, a-r]} u x_{[b+r, \infty)} \in X$. 


For each pair $u,v \in \mathcal{B}_{(b-a)+2r-1}(X)$ with $u_{[a,b]} = w$, let 
\[
E_{u,v} = [v]_{a-r} \cap \{ x \in X \, : x_{(-\infty, a-r]} u x_{[b+r, \infty)} \in X  \}
\]
Then $\bigcup_{u,v} E_{u, v} = X$. In particular, $\mu(E_{u,v}) > 0$ for at least one pair $u,v$. Let $\psi_{u,v,a,b}$ be the holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_X$ that exchanges $u$ and $v$ on $[a,b]$ when possible and does nothing else, as in \S \ref{gibbs-subsec}. By the definition of $E_{u,v}$, we have that for every $x \in E_{u,v}$, $\psi_{u,v,a,b}(x) \in [u]_{a-r}$. Then we have

\begin{align*}
    \mu([w]_a) &\geq \mu([u]_{a-r}) \\
    
    &\geq \mu(\psi_{u,v,a,b}(E_{u,v})) \\
    
    &= \int_{E_{u,v}} D_{\mu, \mathfrak{T}_X}(x, \psi_{u,v,a,b}(x)) \, d\mu(x)  \\
    
    &> 0
\end{align*}

Since $w$ was an arbitrary word at an arbitrary position, $\mu$ has full support.
nodes.statement_short: Use strong irreducibility and compactness to insert any word via a holonomy from a positive-measure set, giving positive measure to every cylinder.

nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant nonsingular measure on $X$. Let $r \geq 1$ be a witness for the strong irreducibility of $X$. Fix $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a < b$, and fix $w \in \mathcal{B}_{b-a}(X)$.

nodes.name: w arbitrary, so mu has full support
nodes.statement: Since $w$ was an arbitrary word at an arbitrary position, $\mu$ has full support.
nodes.statement_short: w arbitrary, so mu has full support

nodes.name: Generalization to countable groups
nodes.statement: The statement and proof of Proposition \ref{strong-irred-support} generalize essentially without modification when $\mathbb{Z}$ is replaced by an arbitrary countable group, with a suitable generalization of strong irreducibility \cite{ceccherini-silberstein-coornaert-2012-periodic, barbieri2018equivalence}. We also mention that strong irreducibility is used in the proof of Proposition \ref{strong-irred-support} to show that all $\mathfrak{T}_X$ equivalence classes are dense in $X$. These equivalence classes are the orbits of the action of the countable group $\Gamma$ generating $\mathfrak{T}_X$. In the special case of a shift of finite type, $\Gamma$ can be taken to be generated by homeomorphisms \cite{meyerovitch2013gibbs}. We can thus interpret Proposition \ref{strong-irred-support} as the statement that a nonsingular measure for a minimal continuous action must have full support.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.4 extends to countable groups; it says nonsingular measures for minimal actions have full support.

nodes.name: Doubly transitive point
nodes.statement:
[doubly transitive point]
Let $X$ be a shift space. A point $x \in X$ is \textit{doubly transitive} if every word $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ appears in $x$ infinitely often to the left and to the right.
differentia: every word $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ appears in $x$ infinitely often to the left and to the right
nodes.label: defn-doub-trans

nodes.name: Doubly transitive points exist iff irreducible
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that a shift space $X$ contains a doubly transitive point if and only if $X$ is irreducible (see \S 9.1, \cite{lind1995introduction} for more details).
conclusions: a shift space $X$ contains a doubly transitive point if and only if $X$ is irreducible
equivalent_conditions: a shift space $X$ contains a doubly transitive point

nodes.name: Doubly transitive points form an invariant set
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a shift space. Then the set $D_X \subset X$ of doubly transitive points is $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a shift space.
conclusions: the set $D_X \subset X$ of doubly transitive points is $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant
nodes.label: lemma-doub-trans-invar

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: If $X$ is not irreducible then $D_X = \emptyset$, which is trivially $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant, so assume that $X$ is irreducible. Let $x \in D_X$ and suppose that $x' \in X$ with $(x,x') \in \mathfrak{T}_X$. Then there exists some $\Delta = [a,b] \cap \mathbb{Z}$ such that $x_{\Delta^c} = x'_{\Delta^c}$. Since $x \in D_X$, every word $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ appears infinitely often both in $x_{(-\infty, a-1]} = x'_{(-\infty, a-1]}$ and in $x_{[b+1, \infty)} = x'_{[b+1, \infty)}$. Therefore $x' \in D_X$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial if X is reducible; otherwise points asymptotic to a doubly transitive point share its tails, so are doubly transitive.

nodes.name: Reducible case is trivial; assume irreducible
nodes.statement: If $X$ is not irreducible then $D_X = \emptyset$, which is trivially $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant, so assume that $X$ is irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: Reducible case is trivial; assume irreducible

nodes.name: Take x' asymptotic to x, agreeing outside a finite window
nodes.statement: Let $x \in D_X$ and suppose that $x' \in X$ with $(x,x') \in \mathfrak{T}_X$. Then there exists some $\Delta = [a,b] \cap \mathbb{Z}$ such that $x_{\Delta^c} = x'_{\Delta^c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take x' asymptotic to x, agreeing outside a finite window

nodes.name: Every word recurs in the shared tails
nodes.statement: Since $x \in D_X$, every word $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ appears infinitely often both in $x_{(-\infty, a-1]} = x'_{(-\infty, a-1]}$ and in $x_{[b+1, \infty)} = x'_{[b+1, \infty)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every word recurs in the shared tails

nodes.name: Conclude x' is doubly transitive
nodes.statement: Therefore $x' \in D_X$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude x' is doubly transitive

nodes.name: Complement of doubly transitive points is invariant
nodes.statement: It is then immediate that $X \setminus D_X$ is also $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant.
conclusions: $X \setminus D_X$ is also $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant

nodes.name: Justification of invariance of the complement
nodes.statement: (In general, if $\mathcal{R}$ is an equivalence relation on $X$ and $A$ is an $\mathcal{R}$-invariant subset, then $A^c$ is also $\mathcal{R}$-invariant.)
nodes.statement_short: Complements of invariant sets of an equivalence relation are invariant.

nodes.name: Doubly transitive points have full measure
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an irreducible shift space and let $\mu$ be a fully supported $\sigma$-invariant ergodic  measure on $X$. Let $D_X$ denote the set of doubly transitive points. Then $\mu(D_X) = 1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Yoo 2018 (proof of Lemma 4.5); generalizes Lind & Marcus Theorem 9.4.9
assumptions: Let $X$ be an irreducible shift space
let $\mu$ be a fully supported $\sigma$-invariant ergodic  measure on $X$
nodes.label: prop-doub-trans-full-meas

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.7
nodes.statement:
Recall that a \textit{generic point}, for a continuous transformation of a compact space with an $\sigma$-invariant measure, is a point that satisfies the conclusion of the pointwise ergodic theorem (Theorem $1.14$, \cite{walters1982ergodic}) for every continuous function. Since $\mu$ is ergodic with respect to $\sigma$, the sets of generic points with respect to $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{-1}$ have full measure (\cite{furstenberg-1981-recurrence}, Proposition 3.7), so their intersection has full measure as well. Since $\mu$ has full support, every point that is generic for both $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{-1}$ (in particular, almost every point in $X$) is doubly transitive. In greater detail: we prove the contrapositive. Suppose $x$ is not doubly transitive. Then there is a word $w$ which appears at most finitely often, without loss of generality to the right, in $x$. Then
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbf{1}_{[w]_0} (\sigma^k x) = 0 \neq \mu([w]_0)
\]
so $x$ does not satisfy the conclusion of the ergodic theorem for the continuous function $\mathbf{1}_{[w]_0}$. Therefore $x$ is not generic for $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Points generic for both sigma and its inverse have full measure, and with full support such points are doubly transitive (contrapositive via ergodic averages).

nodes.name: Points generic for sigma and its inverse have full measure
nodes.statement: Since $\mu$ is ergodic with respect to $\sigma$, the sets of generic points with respect to $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{-1}$ have full measure (\cite{furstenberg-1981-recurrence}, Proposition 3.7), so their intersection has full measure as well.

nodes.statement_short: Such points are doubly transitive

nodes.name: So x is not generic
nodes.statement: Therefore $x$ is not generic for $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Degree of a finite-to-one factor code
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a shift of finite type, let $Y$ be a sofic shift, and let $\pi: X \to Y$ be a finite-to-one factor code. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.9
nodes.statement:
First, for a technical reason described below, we assume that $\pi$ is a one-block code, in the sense that it is induced by a map $\Pi\colon \mathcal{B}_1(X) \to \mathcal{B}_1(Y)$. We assume further that it has a \textit{magic symbol}---that is, a symbol $b \in \mathcal{B}_1(Y)$ with a unique $\Pi$-preimage $a \in \mathcal{B}_1(X)$, such that if $\pi(x)=y$ and $y_0 = b$, then $x_0 = a$. These assumptions incur no loss of generality (\cite{lind1995introduction}, \S9.1).

These assumptions made, we see how to lift holonomies of $\mathfrak{T}_Y$ to holonomies of $\mathfrak{T}_X$. Since $\pi$ is a Borel map between complete separable metric spaces $X,Y$ which restricts to an injection on the Borel set $D_X$, the inverse $\pi|_{D_X}^{-1}: D_Y \to D_X$  is Borel (\cite{kechris1995descriptive}, Theorem 15.1). Now let $\psi: A \to B$ be a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_Y$. Define the map $\Tilde{\psi} : \pi^{-1}(A) \cap D_X \to \pi^{-1}(B) \cap D_X$ by $\Tilde{\psi} = \pi^{-1} \circ \psi \circ \pi$; this is clearly a measurable bijection. 

Moreover, to see that $(x,\Tilde{\psi}(x)) \in \mathfrak{T}_X$  for each $x \in \pi^{-1}(A) \cap D_X$, observe that $(\pi(x), \pi \circ \Tilde{\psi}(x)) = (\pi(x), \psi \circ \pi(x)) \in \mathfrak{T}_Y$, so there exist $m < n$ with $\pi(x)_{[m,n]^c} = \psi \circ \pi(x)_{[m,n]^c}$. Since $\pi(x)$ and $\psi \circ \pi (x)$ are doubly transitive, the magic symbol $b$ for $\pi$ appears infinitely often to the left and right. We may therefore assume, by taking $m$ and $n$ larger if necessary, that
\[
\pi(x)_{m-1} = \psi \circ \pi(x)_{m-1} = b = \pi(x)_{n+1} = \psi \circ \pi(x)_{n+1}
\]
Moreover, since the magic symbol occurs infinitely often to the left and right, any word outside $[m,n]$ appears within a word beginning and ending with $b$. Proposition 9.1.9 in \cite{lind1995introduction} asserts, in the almost invertible case, that such a word has a unique $\pi$-preimage. This shows that $(x,\Tilde{\psi}(x))$ agree outside of $[m,n]$, so $\Tilde{\psi}$ is indeed a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_X$.

Now, let $\Gamma_X, \Gamma_Y$ be countable groups of holonomies generating $\mathfrak{T}_X, \mathfrak{T}_Y$ respectively, and let $A \subset Y$ be Borel with $\nu(A) = 0$. Observe that $\mathfrak{T}_Y(A) = \bigcup_{\gamma \in \Gamma_Y} \gamma(A)$. Observe further that, for each $\gamma \in \Gamma_Y$,
\begin{align*}
    \nu(\gamma(A)) &= \nu( \gamma(A) \setminus D_Y) + \nu( \gamma(A) \cap D_Y   ) \\
    
    &= \mu\left(\pi^{-1}(\gamma(A) \cap D_Y)\right)\\
    
    &= \mu( \Tilde{\gamma} (\pi^{-1}(A \cap D_Y))          ) \\
    
    &= 0
\end{align*}
since $\pi^{-1}(A \cap D_Y)$ is $\mu$-null and $\mu$ is $\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular. Therefore $\nu$ is indeed $\mathfrak{T}_Y$-nonsingular.

Again, let $\psi: A \to B$ be a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_Y$ and let $\Tilde{\psi}$ be as above. Then
\begin{align*}
    \nu(B) &= \mu( \pi^{-1}(\psi(A \cap D_Y))     )     \\
    
    &= \mu(  \Tilde{\psi}(\pi^{-1} (A) \cap D_X )     ) \\
    
    &= \int_{\pi^{-1} (A) \cap D_X} D_{\mu, \mathfrak{T}_X}( x, \Tilde{\psi}(x)   ) \, d\mu(x) \\
    
    &= \int_{A \cap D_Y} D_{\mu, \mathfrak{T}_X}( \pi^{-1}(y), \pi^{-1}(\psi(y))  ) \, d\nu(y),
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from the change of variables formula.

On the other hand, since $\nu$ is $\mathfrak{T}_Y$-nonsingular, we know that
\[
\nu(B) = \int_A D_{\mu, \mathfrak{T}_Y}( y, \psi(y)  ) \, d\nu(y)
\]
By the uniqueness of the Radon-Nikodym derivative, we then have, for almost all $(y,y') \in D_Y^2 \cap \mathfrak{T}_Y$, that $D_{\nu, \mathfrak{T}_Y}(y,y') = D_{\mu, \mathfrak{T}_X}( \pi^{-1}(y), \pi^{-1}(y')  )$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift holonomies of the sofic shift to the SFT on doubly transitive points via a magic symbol. Nonsingularity and the Radon-Nikodym cocycle then transfer by change of variables.

nodes.name: Why the proof does not adapt to finite-to-one codes
nodes.statement: In Corollary \ref{irred-fin-1}, we generalize Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} from almost invertible to finite-to-one codes, in the case that the cocycle on the range is induced by a sufficiently regular potential. It is therefore natural to ask whether the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} can be adapted to the finite-to-one setting. However, such an adaptation would not be straightforward, because at higher degrees we lose a key condition on which the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} relied: namely, that preimages of asymptotic doubly transitive points must themselves be asymptotic. Indeed, if $\pi$ has degree $d > 1$, then every doubly transitive point $y \in Y$ has $d$ preimages, no two of which ever exhibit the same symbol in the same position (see Exercise 9.1.3, \cite{lind1995introduction}), and are therefore about as far from asymptotic as one could imagine.

nodes.statement:
As in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs}, we assume without loss of generality (that is, up to a conjugacy of $X$) that $\pi$ is a one-block code, induced by a block map $\Pi: \mathcal{B}_1(X) \to \mathcal{B}_1(Y)$. We assume further that $\pi$ has a magic symbol $b \in \mathcal{B}_1(Y)$, which has a unique $\Pi$-preimage $a \in \mathcal{B}_1(X)$.

Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant measure on $X$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$; such a $\mu$ exists by Lemma \ref{rel-kry-bog}. We first suppose further that $\mu$ is ergodic. We begin by showing that $\mu$ has full support. Let $w \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ be arbitrary. By irreducibility, there exist $u,v \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ such that $auwva \in \mathcal{B}(X)$. Let $s = \Pi(uwv)$, so that, by the same argument as in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} (using \cite{lind1995introduction}, \S 9.1), $[auwva]_0 = \pi^{-1}([bsb]_0)$. Since $\nu$ has full support by hypothesis, $\nu([bsb]_0) > 0$, so $\mu([w]_0) > 0$, since $[auwva] \subseteq [w]$, with coordinates lined up appropriately. Since $w$ was arbitrary and $\mu$ is $\sigma$-invariant, $\mu$ has full support.


Let $\psi\colon X \to X$ be a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_X$. As in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} (but with the holonomies being pushed in the opposite direction), $\pi$ forms a Borel isomorphism between $D_X$ and $D_Y$, and if $x,x' \in D_X$ then $(x,x') \in \mathfrak{T}_X$ if and only if $(\pi(x),\pi(x')) \in \mathfrak{T}_Y$. Therefore, we have a holonomy $\Tilde{\psi} = \pi \circ \psi \circ (\pi|_{D_X})^{-1} : D_Y \to D_Y$ of $\mathfrak{T}_Y$.

Let $N \subset X$ be a Borel set with $\mu$-measure zero. Observe that 
\[
\psi(N) = \psi(N \cap D_X) \cup \psi(N \setminus D_X) 
\]


This yields that $\mu(\psi(N)) = \mu(\psi(N) \cap D_X)$, since $\psi(N \setminus D_X) = \psi(N)\setminus D_X$, and $D_X$ has full measure by ergodicity and Proposition \ref{prop-doub-trans-full-meas}. Moreover, 
\[
\psi(N \cap D_X) = \pi^{-1} \circ \Tilde{\psi} ( \pi(N) \cap D_Y )
\]
Now, $\nu(\pi(N) \cap D_Y) = \mu(N \cap D_X) = 0$, so $\nu(\Tilde{\psi} ( \pi(N) \cap D_Y ))$ = 0, since $\nu$ is $\mathfrak{T}_Y$-nonsingular. Therefore $\mu(\psi(N \cap D_X)) = 0$ as well, so in fact $\mu(\psi(N)) = 0$, which shows that $\mu$ is indeed 
$\mathfrak{T}_X$-nonsingular. A calculation in the same spirit, very similar to the calculation that concludes the proof of Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs}, shows that $\mu$ is Gibbs for $\phi \circ (\pi \times \pi)$, as claimed. This concludes the proof for $\mu$ ergodic; the general case follows by convexity.

nodes.name: Topological pressure and equilibrium measure
nodes.statement:
[topological pressure and equilibrium states]
Let $X$ be a shift space and let $f\colon X \to \mathbb{R} $ be a continuous function. The \textit{topological pressure} of $f$ is the value
\[
P_X(\sigma, f) = \sup \left\{ h(\mu) + \int_X f \, d\mu\right\}
\]
where the supremum is over all $\sigma$-invariant measures $\mu$ on $X$. Any measure $\mu$ attaining the supremum is known as an \textit{equilibrium measure} for $f$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited; variational form as in Keller 1998)
nodes.statement_short: Pressure is the sup of entropy plus integral of f over invariant measures; maximizers are equilibrium measures.

nodes.name: Summable variation space SV(X)
nodes.statement:
[the function space $\mathrm{SV}(X)$]
Let $X$ be a shift space and let $f\colon X \to \mathbb{R} $ be a continuous function. We define the \textit{$k^{\text{th}}$ variation} of $f$ as
\[
v_k(f) = \sup \{ | f(x) - f(y) | \, : \, x_{[-k,k]} = y_{[-k,k]} \}
\]
for $k \geq 0$; it is convenient to define $\mathrm{var}_{-1}(f) = \| f \|_{\infty}$. We then define
\[
\SVnorm{f}{X} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}  v_{k-1}(f)
\]
and define the class of potentials $\mathrm{SV}(X) = \{ f \in C(X) \, : \,  \SVnorm{f}{X} < \infty   \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Potentials whose sequence of variations is summable.
nodes.label: SV-space

nodes.name: Cocycle induced by a potential
nodes.statement:
It is easy to verify that $\left(\mathrm{SV}(X), \SVnorm{\cdot}{X} \right)$ is a Banach space, and that (\cite{meyerovitch2013gibbs}, \cite{borsato2020conformal}) a potential $f \in \mathrm{SV}(X)$ defines a cocycle $\phi_f$ on $\mathfrak{T}_X$ via the following absolutely convergent series:
\[
\phi_f(x,y) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} [ f(\sigma^n y) - f(\sigma^n x)  ]
\]
nodes.statement_short: SV(X) is a Banach space and each f in SV(X) defines a cocycle phi_f by summing differences along the orbit.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.5
nodes.statement:
When $X$ is a mixing shift of finite type, the result follows from Theorem \ref{lf} and Proposition \ref{strong-irred-support}. Now, let $X$ be an irreducible shift of finite type such that $X$ has period $p$. We decompose $X$ into $p$ cyclically moving classes (see \cite{lind1995introduction}, \S 4.5), i.e., $X = \sqcup_{i=0}^{p-1} X_i$ where $\sigma(X_i) = X_{i+1 \mod p}$ and each $X_i$ is mixing with respect to $\sigma^p$. In particular, $\sigma^p$ is a homeomorphism of each clopen set $X_i$; the system $(X, \sigma^p)$ is known as the $p^{\text{th}}$ higher power shift of $X$ (\cite{lind1995introduction}, \S 1.4), and the $X_i$ are its cyclically moving classes. 

There is a bijection between $\sigma$-invariant measures $\mu$ on $X$ and $\sigma^p$-invariant measures $\mu'$ on $X_0$, which is given by normalized restriction in one direction and averaging in the other. That is, we take $\mu' = p \mu|_{X_0}$ and $\mu = p^{-1 }\sum_{j=0}^{p-1} \sigma^{j}_* \mu'$. Observe that $\mu$ has full support if and only if $\mu'$ does. 

Moreover, we have
\[ h_X(\mu) + \int_X f \, d\mu = \frac{1}{p} \left( h_{X_0}(\mu') + \int_{X_0} R_p f \, d\mu'         \right)
\]
where $R_p f =  \sum_{j=0}^{p-1} f \circ \sigma^{-j}$. Therefore $\mu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$ on $X$ precisely when $\mu'$ is an equilibrium measure for $R_p f$ on $X_0$. So far, our discussion is essentially identical to Yoo's.


We now need to show that $R_p f \in \mathrm{SV}(X_0)$; this is where we part from Yoo, who considers a different class of potentials.  Observe that, for each $j \in \{0, \dots, p-1\}$, the $k$-th variation of a function on $X_0$ behaves like the $kp$-th variation of that function on $X$, so we have
\[
\SVnorm{f \circ \sigma^{-j}}{X_0} \leq \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} v_{kp}(f \circ \sigma^{-j}) \leq \frac{1}{p} \SVnorm{f \circ \sigma^{-j}}{X}
\]
It is also easy to check that $\mathrm{SV}(X)$ is closed under translation, showing that indeed $R_p f \in \mathrm{SV}(X_0)$. 

Let $\mu$  be an equilibrium measure for $f$. Then the unique $\mu'$ on $X_0$ such that $\mu = p^{-1 }\sum_{j=0}^{p-1} \sigma^{j}_* \mu'$ is an equilibrium measure for $R_p f$; since $X_0$ is mixing, $\mu'$ is fully supported. Thus $\mu$ is fully supported as well.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement:
By Lemma \ref{rel-kry-bog}, there exists a $\sigma$-invariant measure $\mu$ on $X$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$, and we can choose $\mu$ to be ergodic whenever $\nu$ is ergodic. We now show that any such $\mu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f \circ \pi$. Since $\pi$ is finite-to-one, the Abramov-Rokhlin formula \cite{adler1963skew} shows that $h(\mu) = h(\nu)$. Then
\[
    h(\mu) + \int_X f \circ \pi \, d\mu = h(\nu) + \int_Y f \, d\nu = P_Y(\sigma, f)
\]
We need to show that $P_X(\sigma, f \circ \pi) = P_Y(\sigma, f)$. Clearly $P_X(\sigma, f \circ \pi) \geq P_Y(\sigma, f)$, so we only need the reverse inequality. Let $\lambda$ be any $\sigma$-invariant measure on $X$. Again $h(\pi_* \lambda) = h(\lambda)$ by the Abramov-Rokhlin formula, so we have

\[
    h(\lambda) + \int_X f \circ \pi \, d\lambda = h(\pi_* \lambda) + \int_Y f \, d\pi_* \lambda \leq P_Y(f)
\]
Therefore $P_X(\sigma, f \circ \pi) = P_Y(\sigma, f)$, so $\mu$ is indeed an equilibrium measure for $f \circ \pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift via the relative Krylov-Bogliubov lemma; the Abramov-Rokhlin formula preserves entropy so pressures agree.

nodes.statement:
Since $Y$ is an irreducible sofic shift, there exist an irreducible shift of finite type $X$ and an almost invertible factor code $\pi\colon X \to Y$, for instance the minimal right-resolving presentation (\cite{lind1995introduction}, \S 3.3, \S 9.2). 

Suppose first that $\nu$ is ergodic. By Lemma \ref{lift-eqm}, there exists an ergodic equilibrium measure $\mu$ for $f \circ \pi$ such that $\nu = \pi_{*}\mu$.  Then, by Theorem \ref{lf}, $\mu$ is a Gibbs measure for $f \circ \pi$, and by Proposition \ref{yoo-sv}, $\mu$ has full support.  Then, by Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs}, which requires ergodicity and full support, $\nu$ is a Gibbs measure for $f$.

The general result follows from the ergodic case via the Krein-Milman theorem \cite{simon2011convexity}, together with the compactness and convexity of the sets of Gibbs and equilibrium measures \cite{keller1998equilibrium} and the fact that the extreme points of these sets are precisely their ergodic elements.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.9
nodes.statement:
Let $X$ have period $p$ and let $X_0, \dots, X_{p-1}$ be the cyclically moving classes of $X$ as in the proof of Proposition \ref{yoo-sv}. Note that each $X_i$, $0 \leq i \leq p-1$ is $\mathfrak{T}_X$-invariant and that we can regard each one as a mixing shift of finite type with alphabet a subset of $\mathcal{B}_p(X)$, so that it is meaningful to speak of the Gibbs relations $\mathfrak{T}_{X_i}$. Moreover, since each class $X_i$ is $\mathfrak{T}_{X}$-invariant, we have for each $i$ that $\mathfrak{T}_{X_i}$ is simply the restriction of $\mathfrak{T}_X$ to $X_i \times X_i$.

Let $\mu$ be a Gibbs measure for $f$ and  $\mu'$ be the normalized restriction of $\mu$ of $X$ to $X_0$, i.e., $\mu'(E) = p \mu(E)$ for any Borel set $E \subseteq X_0$. Lemma \ref{lemma-period-trans} shows that every holonomy $\psi: A \to B$ of $\mathfrak{T}_X$  restricts to a holonomy $\psi_0 : A \cap X_0 \to B \cap X_0$ of the relation $\mathfrak{T}_{X_0}$. Moreover, every holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_{X_0}$ clearly arises as such a restriction: if $\psi_0$ is a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_{X_0}$, $\psi_0 = \psi|_{X_0}$ where $\psi|_{X_i} = \sigma^i \circ \psi_0 \circ \sigma^{-i}$. Therefore the measure $\mu'$ inherits the Gibbsianness of $\mu$, with respect to $R_p f =  \sum_{j=0}^{p-1} f \circ \sigma^j$. Since each $X_i$, $0 \leq i \leq p-1$ is a mixing shift of finite type, therefore strongly irreducible, Theorem \ref{dobrushin} shows that $\mu'$ is an equilibrium measure for $R_p f$. As in the proof of Proposition \ref{yoo-sv}, we have 
\[
h_X(\mu) + \int_X f \, d\mu = \frac{1}{p} \left( h_{X_0}(\mu') + \int_{X_0} R_p f \, d\mu'         \right),
\]
which concludes that $\mu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$.

nodes.name: Restrict mu to X_0; holonomies correspond by Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a Gibbs measure for $f$ and  $\mu'$ be the normalized restriction of $\mu$ of $X$ to $X_0$, i.e., $\mu'(E) = p \mu(E)$ for any Borel set $E \subseteq X_0$. Lemma \ref{lemma-period-trans} shows that every holonomy $\psi: A \to B$ of $\mathfrak{T}_X$  restricts to a holonomy $\psi_0 : A \cap X_0 \to B \cap X_0$ of the relation $\mathfrak{T}_{X_0}$. Moreover, every holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_{X_0}$ clearly arises as such a restriction: if $\psi_0$ is a holonomy of $\mathfrak{T}_{X_0}$, $\psi_0 = \psi|_{X_0}$ where $\psi|_{X_i} = \sigma^i \circ \psi_0 \circ \sigma^{-i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict mu to X_0; holonomies correspond by Lemma 4.8

nodes.name: mu' is Gibbs for R_p f
nodes.statement: Therefore the measure $\mu'$ inherits the Gibbsianness of $\mu$, with respect to $R_p f =  \sum_{j=0}^{p-1} f \circ \sigma^j$.
nodes.statement_short: mu' is Gibbs for R_p f

nodes.name: Classical Dobrushin on X_0
nodes.statement: Since each $X_i$, $0 \leq i \leq p-1$ is a mixing shift of finite type, therefore strongly irreducible, Theorem \ref{dobrushin} shows that $\mu'$ is an equilibrium measure for $R_p f$.
nodes.statement_short: Classical Dobrushin on X_0

nodes.name: Pressure identity transfers back to mu
nodes.statement:
As in the proof of Proposition \ref{yoo-sv}, we have 
\[
h_X(\mu) + \int_X f \, d\mu = \frac{1}{p} \left( h_{X_0}(\mu') + \int_{X_0} R_p f \, d\mu'         \right),
\]
which concludes that $\mu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Pressure identity transfers back to mu

nodes.name: Preservation of Gibbsianness for finite-to-one factor codes
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an irreducible shift of finite type and $Y$ an irreducible sofic shift. Let $\pi: X \to Y$ be a finite-to-one factor code, let $f\colon Y \to \mathbb{R}$  be a potential with summable variation, that is, $f \in SV(Y)$, and let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure for $f \circ \pi$. Then $\nu = \pi_* \mu$ is a Gibbs measure for $f$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be an irreducible shift of finite type
$Y$ an irreducible sofic shift
Let $\pi: X \to Y$ be a finite-to-one factor code
let $f\colon Y \to \mathbb{R}$  be a potential with summable variation, that is, $f \in SV(Y)$
let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure for $f \circ \pi$
conclusions: $\nu = \pi_* \mu$ is a Gibbs measure for $f$
nodes.label: irred-fin-1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.10
nodes.statement: First note that $\mu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f \circ \pi$ by Lemma \ref{dobrushin-irred-sft}. Since $\pi$ is finite-to-one, $\nu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$ (\cite{yoo2018decomposition}, Lemma 4.4), so by Theorem \ref{sofic-lf}, $\nu$ is Gibbs for $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Gibbs implies equilibrium upstairs (Lemma 4.9), equilibrium pushes down (Yoo), and Theorem 4.7 gives Gibbs downstairs.

nodes.name: Scope of the generalization of Proposition 3.9
nodes.statement: While Corollary \ref{irred-fin-1} may look like it generalizes Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} in that $\mu$ need no longer be ergodic and $\pi$ need no longer have degree one. However, the cocycle in Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} need not a priori be induced by the pullback of a potential with summable variation. Corollary \ref{irred-fin-1} therefore generalizes Proposition \ref{prop-pres-gibbs} only in this special case.

nodes.name: Dobrushin theorem for irreducible sofic shifts
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be an irreducible sofic shift and let $f\colon Y \to \mathbb{R}$  be a potential with summable variation, that is, $f \in SV(Y)$. Let $\nu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure for $f$. Then $\nu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$.
assumptions: Let $Y$ be an irreducible sofic shift
let $f\colon Y \to \mathbb{R}$  be a potential with summable variation, that is, $f \in SV(Y)$
Let $\nu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure for $f$.
conclusions: $\nu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$.
nodes.label: sofic-dobrushin

nodes.name: Ergodic case; take minimal right-resolving presentation
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\nu$ is ergodic. Let $\pi: X \to Y$ be the minimal right-resolving presentation of $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Ergodic case; take minimal right-resolving presentation

nodes.name: Lift to an ergodic Gibbs measure (Prop 3.11)
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{sofic-gibbs-pushfwd}, there exists an ergodic $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure $\mu$ for $f \circ \pi$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift to an ergodic Gibbs measure (Prop 3.11)

nodes.name: Dobrushin for irreducible SFTs upstairs
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{dobrushin-irred-sft}, $\mu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f \circ \pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Dobrushin for irreducible SFTs upstairs

nodes.name: Push down equilibrium measure (Yoo Lemma 4.4)
nodes.statement: Finally, again by Lemma 4.4 in \cite{yoo2018decomposition}, $\nu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Push down equilibrium measure (Yoo Lemma 4.4)

nodes.name: General case by compactness and convexity
nodes.statement: The result for general (not necessarily ergodic) $\nu$ follows from the ergodic case by compactness and convexity as in the proof of Theorem \ref{sofic-lf}.
nodes.statement_short: General case by compactness and convexity

nodes.name: Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle theorem for irreducible sofic shifts
nodes.statement: Taken together, Theorems \ref{sofic-lf} and \ref{sofic-dobrushin} show that for a potential with summable variations on an irreducible sofic shift, the equilibrium measures are precisely the $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measures.
assumptions: a potential with summable variations on an irreducible sofic shift
conclusions: the equilibrium measures are precisely the $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measures

nodes.name: Lifting Gibbs measures through finite-to-one factor codes
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an irreducible shift of finite type and $Y$ an irreducible sofic shift. Let $\pi: X \to Y$ be a finite-to-one factor code, let $f\colon Y \to \mathbb{R}$  be a potential with summable variation, that is, $f \in SV(Y)$, and let $\nu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure for $f$. Then there exists a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure $\mu$ for $f \circ \pi$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be an irreducible shift of finite type
$Y$ an irreducible sofic shift
Let $\pi: X \to Y$ be a finite-to-one factor code
let $f\colon Y \to \mathbb{R}$  be a potential with summable variation, that is, $f \in SV(Y)$
let $\nu$ be a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure for $f$
conclusions: there exists a $\sigma$-invariant Gibbs measure $\mu$ for $f \circ \pi$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$
nodes.label: lift-gibbs-fin-1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.12
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{sofic-dobrushin}, $\nu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$. By Lemma \ref{lift-eqm}, there is an equilibrium measure $\mu$ for $f \circ \pi$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$. By Theorem \ref{lf}, $\mu$ is a Gibbs measure for $f \circ \pi$, and is certainly $\sigma$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: Gibbs implies equilibrium (Theorem 4.11), lift the equilibrium measure (Lemma 4.6), and apply Lanford-Ruelle upstairs.

nodes.name: Gibbs implies equilibrium (Theorem 4.11)
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{sofic-dobrushin}, $\nu$ is an equilibrium measure for $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Gibbs implies equilibrium (Theorem 4.11)

nodes.name: Lift the equilibrium measure (Lemma 4.6)
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lift-eqm}, there is an equilibrium measure $\mu$ for $f \circ \pi$ with $\pi_* \mu = \nu$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the equilibrium measure (Lemma 4.6)

nodes.name: Lanford-Ruelle upstairs
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{lf}, $\mu$ is a Gibbs measure for $f \circ \pi$, and is certainly $\sigma$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: Lanford-Ruelle upstairs

nodes.name: Existence of finite-to-one factor codes onto a sofic shift
nodes.statement: In closing, we note that it is an open problem to determine the existence of a finite-to-one factor code from a given shift of finite type $X$ onto a given sofic shift $Y$, as in the hypotheses of Corollaries \ref{irred-fin-1} and \ref{lift-gibbs-fin-1}.
